extracted.intended_audience: USCIS adjudicators, immigration attorneys, visa/adjustment applicants, and public commenters on the DHS proposed public charge rule
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for determining whether an alien is likely to become a public charge under the DHS/USCIS proposed rule, including evidentiary requirements, heavily weighed factors, and treatment of affidavits of support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and skills as a factor (positive for self-sufficiency)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS considers an alien's education and skills as positive factors for evidencing self-sufficiency and reducing likelihood of becoming a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule explains that higher educational attainment and professional/educational credentials correlate with lower public benefit participation; DHS may consider academic degrees, certifications, occupational skills, licenses, and other credentials. The document cites SIPP and Census data showing those with certificates/licenses or higher education have lower rates of cash and non-cash benefit receipt. DHS would give appropriate consideration to market demand for proficiencies in languages other than English.

rubrics_metrics.name: USCIS evidentiary requirements for education/skills and language proficiencies
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS proposes considering certain types of evidence when reviewing the education and skills factor, including employment history, academic degrees/certifications, occupational skills/certifications/licenses, and English or other language proficiencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS states review would include, but not be limited to: evidence of recent history of employment; academic degree or certifications (including high school or equivalent) or higher; occupational skills, certifications, or licenses; and proficiency in English or proficiencies in additional languages. Examples, definitions, and references to working definitions (e.g., GEMEnA) are provided. The rule also notes that DHS may consider proficiency in other languages with attention to market demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of prospective immigration status and expected period of admission
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS would take into account the immigration status, duration of admission sought, and classification the alien is seeking as part of the totality of the circumstances for public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule explains that evidence required of immigrants vs nonimmigrants may differ in scope; permanent residents may be eligible for certain public benefits upon entry or after five years, which increases the possibility they would avail themselves of benefits; nonimmigrants coming temporarily (e.g., B-2 visitors for two weeks) are generally less likely to use benefits. DHS would consider these possibilities in the totality of the circumstances, and evidence may exist that gives rise to a public charge concern even for nonimmigrants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of support filing requirement and failure consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain aliens required to submit an affidavit of support who fail to do so will be inadmissible on public charge grounds without review of other statutory factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule cites INA sections 212(a)(4)(C)/(D): failure to submit a required affidavit of support necessarily results in a determination of inadmissibility based on the public charge ground. Certain categories are exempt; references and cross-citations to the statute and forms (I-864, I-864EZ) are included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting of affidavits of support and sponsor assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: A sponsor's facially sufficient affidavit of support is a positive factor but will not be outcome-determinative; DHS will assess the sponsor's ability and likelihood to provide long-term support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining weight to give an affidavit, USCIS would assess the sponsor's annual income, assets, resources, financial status, relationship to applicant, likelihood the sponsor would provide support, cohabitation, whether the sponsor has submitted affidavits for other individuals, and any other related considerations. The sponsor generally must demonstrate ability to maintain the sponsored alien at an annual income of not less than 125 percent of the FPG. DHS may request additional information or interview the sponsor. Inability or unwillingness of the sponsor to support the alien may be viewed negatively. A sufficient affidavit alone does not eliminate need to consider mandatory factors under the totality of the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heavily weighed factors — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes certain factors or factual circumstances that would generally weigh heavily in public charge determinations, but presence of any one enumerated circumstance would not alone be determinative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A heavily weighed factor could be outweighed by countervailing evidence under the totality of the circumstances. Other negative and positive factors, including those not enumerated, may also be weighed heavily in individual determinations as warranted. Proposed regulatory citation: 8 CFR 212.22.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of employability as a heavily weighed negative factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of current employment, employment history, or a reasonable prospect of future employment (for an alien who is not a full-time student and is authorized to work) is proposed as a heavily weighed negative factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS explains self-sufficiency generally involves being capable and willing to work and maintain gainful employment; a person capable of work who does not work demonstrates lack of self-sufficiency. The rule notes studies linking employment status to lower benefit receipt. Exception: for full-time students the absence of employment is not counted as a heavily weighed negative factor because students are working toward degrees that increase future employability. DHS also recognizes assets/resources (including household members' income) may overcome a negative related to lack of employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Current receipt of one or more public benefits as a heavily weighed negative factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Current receipt of one or more public benefits (as defined in proposed 8 CFR 212.21(b)) is a heavily weighed negative factor in public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule explains current receipt of benefits indicates the alien is currently a public charge under the proposed definition and suggests a likelihood of continued receipt in the future, but current receipt alone would not justify a finding of inadmissibility. DHS cites research on program participation duration and notes that many program participants remain on assistance for extended periods; however, studies do not directly address return-to-program behavior. Proposed regulatory citation: 8 CFR 212.22(c)(1)(ii) and proposed 8 CFR 212.21(b).
